The log of the daily high/low range, averaged over the past 3 days and negated, gives a rank IC of +0.0612 and an incremental IC of +0.0220 (t = 9.0), meaning about 2% of the signal survives after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum. The sign is consistent across all three periods (+0.0315 / +0.0182 / +0.0210), so it is not a single-period artifact. Shorter windows help up to 3 days but 2 days is worse, so the effect is a short-horizon one rather than a persistent one.

Now the incremental IC is −0.0116 with t = −5.4, and it is negative in every sub-period (2022H2 −0.0147, 2023 −0.0172, 2024 −0.0044), so the idea does not hold on this history: coins closing far above their own average close actually underperform next day, and that is consistent across all three periods. I'll stop here rather than spend more tests on the same idea.

What I found: the plain 5-day return is exactly the short-term reversal style that gets removed, so it has no incremental content at all (0.0000), and the smoothed versions of it give the same result. Measuring the close relative to the coin's own average close, however, leaves a real but inverted signal: −0.0116 incremental IC with t = −5.4, negative in every sub-period, so the idea as stated does not hold on 2022–2024; it is the opposite of what the idea claims, and I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: a close near the high means buyers pushed the price up. The range is high/low, so I'll divide the close by it, which is a ratio and therefore comparable across coins regardless of price unit. A ratio close at 1 means the close was exactly at the high; I'll start with a 5-day mean so a single day's noise doesn't dominate.

One more distinct reading of the same idea: the close's position inside the range measured as a percentile within its own recent history, which keeps the same "near the high" meaning but asks whether the coin's typical closing sits high in its own range.

What I found: measuring the close's position inside the day's range as a 5-day mean gives +0.0103 incremental IC with t = 3.0 and the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it isn't a single-period artifact. The median and percentile variants both gave the same best value, so the result is not an outlier effect. I hand in the simplest form, keeping the direction the idea states (a close near the high is bullish).

The idea is about dollar-volume, not price-volume: how much a coin moves in USDT is what matters, and the sign is negative. I'll start with the simplest version — the negative of the 20-day average of `quote_volume` — to see how much of it survives once liquidity is removed.

The raw level is mostly the liquidity style — incremental IC is only 0.0011 with 2023 flipping sign. So I'll measure the same idea as a coin's dollar-volume *relative to its own past*, which captures "trading unusually little" rather than "it is a quiet coin in absolute terms".

The 3-day window gives the same incremental IC as the 5-day one (+0.0096), so the window choice is not the lever — I'll stop here rather than spend the last test on window tuning.

What I found: the idea holds on this history but only in its relative form. The level of dollar-volume is almost entirely the liquidity style — its incremental IC is 0.0011 — while measuring recent dollar-volume against the coin's own 60-day baseline gives +0.0096 incremental IC with t = 3.3 and the same positive sign in all three periods (2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014). The 5-day and 3-day windows are interchangeable, so I hand in the 5-day version as the simpler expression.

The idea is a one-day reversal: coins that fell yesterday should bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is low. The simplest faithful form is minus yesterday's return. I'll test that first to see how much survives after the known short-term reversal style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw one-day reversal is exactly the style that's already been removed, so incremental IC is zero — the idea's own content lives only in the residual. The bounce is about a fall relative to the coin's own normal daily move, so next I'll measure yesterday's return against the coin's own 20-day return volatility, which keeps the same direction but asks "how unusual was yesterday's fall for this coin".

Volatility scaling barely moved the residual (−0.0001), so the magnitude of yesterday's fall isn't what carries the bounce. Since the idea is about the fall itself, I'll keep the magnitude but ask "how big was yesterday's fall compared with the coin's typical daily move", i.e. the fall as a fraction of the coin's own 20-day return volatility.

Two forms in a row now sit at the same place: the volatility-scaled version and the volatility-scaled version of the same quantity, both exactly zero incrementally, with the second having a negative sign in 2024. That's two tests in a row that fail to improve on the best result, so I'll stop rather than keep hunting for a third form.

What I found: the plain one-day reversal is fully absorbed by the known short-term reversal style — its incremental IC is exactly zero, so "coins that fell yesterday bounce" as a raw one-day statement carries nothing on this history. Measuring the fall against the coin's own 20-day return volatility, or as a fraction of its own typical daily move, also leaves nothing, which suggests the bounce is not a residual effect here but a style that is already priced in. The direction stays as the idea states it, and the honest result is that this idea looks wrong on this history.

The direction is as the idea states: coins whose closes sit near their high, i.e. whose buyers dominate the session, score higher.

The idea is about average trade size — USDT traded per trade — so I'll start with the plainest form: the recent average of `quote_volume / num_trades`, negated, since a jump in trade size is bearish. I'll use a short window (5 days, min_periods 4) because "sudden" implies a recent burst.

The plain level of average trade size is essentially flat after the known styles — its absolute IC is +0.022 but it is entirely absorbed. So I need a form that captures a *jump relative to the coin's own normal trade size*, which is what "big players selling out" should mean. I'll take the 5-day mean of `quote_volume / num_trades` and subtract its 60-day mean, negated.

The relative form is also essentially flat (−0.0018), so a single-day spike in trade size is not what carries the signal. The idea is about a *sudden* jump, so I'll measure the same jump more robustly: the 5-day mean of log average trade size minus its 60-day mean, which is bounded and less sensitive to a few huge days.

So the honest reading is that, on this history, a jump in average trade size carries no incremental information beyond liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — big players selling out does not predict underperformance. I'll keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase the score, and hand in the simplest form, which had the most stable (if slightly negative) incremental IC across the three periods.

The idea is about the daily close-above-open gap: a coin that closes far above its open should keep rising. The plainest reading is the log ratio of close to open (unit-free, so comparable across coins), smoothed over a few days to cut single-day noise. I'll start there.

The best-behaved variant is the median, so I hand that one in, keeping the direction the idea states: a coin that closes far above its open scores high, and I am not flipping the sign.

The idea says: a coin whose dollar volume just peaked relative to its own recent past should fall back. The natural measure is the ratio of a short-window mean dollar volume to a longer-window mean, which is a ratio of two USDT-denominated quantities, so it is comparable across coins regardless of price unit. I'll start with the simplest version: 5-day mean divided by a 60-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The ratio gives incremental IC −0.0096 with a t of −3.3, and the sign is consistent across all three periods (2022H2, 2023, 2024), so the idea holds in direction but with the opposite sign to the claim: coins whose volume just hit a high keep outperforming, not falling back. Before concluding, I'll check whether the idea is better captured by a different form of "just hit a high" — a recent peak measured against the coin's own longer-run average rather than a mean-to-mean ratio.
